sections.title: Some
sections.content:
Before plural and uncountable nouns we sometimes use some or zero article (i.e. no article) with very little difference in meaning:
• 'Where were you last week?' 'I was visiting (some) friends.'
• Before serving, pour (some) yoghurt over the top.
With both some and zero article, we are referring to particular people or things but in an indefinite way. We don't use some to make general statements about whole classes of things or people:
• Machinery can be dangerous unless used properly. (not Some machinery ... unless referring to a subset)
• Babies need a lot of attention.

sections.title: Some before numbers
sections.content:
Some is used before a number to mean 'approximately':
• Some eighty per cent of all residents took part in the vote. (= approximately eighty per cent)

sections.title: Some with a singular noun
sections.content:
When we don't know, can't remember, or it is not important exactly which person or thing we are talking about, we can use some instead of a / an with a singular noun.
• He was interrupted twice by some troublemaker in the audience.
We use the phrase some (thing) or other in a similar way:
• I bought them from some shop or other in New Street. (not ... from a shop or other ...)

sections.title: Any vs Some in negative contexts
sections.content:
We usually use any not some (and anyone, anything, etc. not someone, something, etc.) in non-affirmative contexts to refer to non-specific, unspecified things. We generally use any in sentences with a negative meaning:
• There's hardly any sugar left.
• I closed the windows to prevent any flies getting in.
Also with: barely, never, rarely, scarcely, seldom; deny, fail, forbid, prohibit, refuse; reluctant, unable, unlikely.
However, we use some with these negative words:
- when some has the implication 'not all':
• I talk to colleagues before I make some decisions, but I had to make this one on my own.
- when the basic meaning is positive:
• Somebody isn't telling the truth. (= There is some person [who isn't telling the truth])
- when we are talking about a particular but unspecified person or thing:
• I was reluctant to repeat something so critical of Paul. (= a specific criticism)

sections.title: Any with before and comparisons
sections.content:
We often use any in clauses that begin with before, and with comparisons:
• I cleared up the mess before anyone saw it. ('... before someone saw it' suggests that I have a particular person in mind who might see it)
• The material felt softer than anything she had ever touched before.
Anything can be used in clauses where some words have been left out:
• Anything you need, just ask. (= If there is anything you need...)

exercises.question: Sports are dangerous. (Correct this sentence if necessary)
exercises.hint: When not referring to the whole class of things, we use 'some' to refer to a subset.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Some sports are dangerous.
When not referring to the whole class of things, we use 'some' to refer to a subset.

exercises.sentence: Would you like any more coffee? There's plenty left.
exercises.correction: Would you like some more coffee? There's plenty left.
acceptable: Would you like some more coffee?
exercises.hint: In offers, use 'some' (not 'any') — 'some' makes the offer sound genuine and positive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Would you like some more coffee?
In offers and requests where the speaker expects or hopes for a 'yes' answer, use 'some', not 'any'. 'Any' in questions is neutral or suggests doubt. 'Some' in questions softens and invites acceptance: 'Would you like some tea?' sounds welcoming; 'Would you like any tea?' sounds more indifferent.

exercises.question: 250 people charged with assault following Molton riots. (Rewrite using 'some' to mean 'approximately')
exercises.hint: 'Some' can be used before a number to mean approximately.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Some 250 people have been charged...
'Some' can be used before a number to mean approximately. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.sentence: I don't have some money on me — could you lend me a few pounds?
exercises.correction: I don't have any money on me — could you lend me a few pounds?
acceptable: I don't have any money on me
exercises.explanation:
Answer: I don't have any money on me
In negative sentences, use 'any' (not 'some'): 'I don't have any money', 'There isn't any time left', 'She hasn't eaten any breakfast'. 'Some' in negatives ('I don't have some money') sounds incorrect in standard English. The pattern: affirmative → some; negative → any; questions → any (neutral) or some (offer).

exercises.question: I don't know where I got the information from. I must have heard it on ___ radio programme (or other).
exercises.hint: When we don't remember exactly which one, we can use 'some' with a singular noun.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: some
When we don't remember exactly which one, we can use 'some' with a singular noun.

exercises.sentence: Is there some problem with the connection? It keeps dropping.
exercises.correction: Is there any problem with the connection? It keeps dropping.
acceptable: Is there any problem with the connection?
Is something wrong with the connection?
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Is there any problem with the connection?
In neutral questions — where you don't know the answer and aren't making an offer — use 'any': 'Is there any problem?', 'Do you have any questions?', 'Has anyone called?' Use 'some' in questions only when making an offer or when you expect the answer to be yes.

exercises.question: Elias worked hard at learning Japanese but failed to make ___ real progress.
exercises.hint: Use 'any' in a non-affirmative context (after 'failed to').
exercises.explanation:
Answer: any
Use 'any' in a non-affirmative context (after 'failed to').

exercises.question: I was unable to eat ___ of the food.
exercises.hint: 'any' means none of it; 'some' means you couldn't eat a portion of it.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: any / some
'any' means none of it; 'some' means you couldn't eat a portion of it.
